Question fourteen. What is Simpson's paradox? A trend in the total can reverse inside every group. In the kidney stone study, treatment A wins for small stones and for large ones, yet loses overall: seventy-eight percent against eighty-three. A was given mostly to large stones, the hard cases. So segment before you conclude. Question fifteen. How do you avoid a misleading ratio metric? Watch the numerator and the denominator together: revenue per session can rise because sessions fell. And an average of averages isn't the overall average. Five regional averages average sixty-eight. Per customer, it's fifty-two, because one region has only forty customers.

Four short ones to finish. A conversion rate in SQL: count distinct converted users, times one point zero, over distinct users. Without distinct, a repeat purchase counts twice, and point four becomes point six. The one point zero stops some databases dividing whole numbers down to zero. A novelty effect is a lift that comes from newness, and fades. In week one, the change that's about to vanish looks best: fourteen percent against four. A primacy effect is the reverse, when people resist a change at first. Either way, run the test long enough to see it settle. A cohort analysis groups users by when they started, like their sign-up month, and follows each group. Here every cohort keeps more than the last: twenty-six percent at week eight for January, fifty-two for May. And a retention curve is the share of a cohort still active each week. A healthy one flattens onto a plateau. For two weeks these two match. By week twelve, one keeps thirty-one percent, and the other two. An assistant can now draft every one of these answers in seconds. Knowing which drafts to trust is the last round. Next: A I-assisted analysis.
